OpenClaw 2026.4.10 Changelog Deep Dive: Native Codex Integration, Active Memory & Local MLX Voice

Apr 11, 2026
Vibe Sparking

Overview

Section titled “Overview”

2026.4.10 is a heavyweight release, shipped on April 11, 2026. It contains 17 new features and 20+ fixes, covering model integration, memory systems, voice, security hardening, and multi-channel fixes.

Three highlights:

  1. Native Codex Integration — OpenAI Codex as a built-in provider, independent from the OpenAI channel
  2. Active Memory Plugin — Automatic memory recall without manual user triggers
  3. Local MLX Voice — macOS Talk Mode supports local MLX voice inference

New Features

Section titled “New Features”

1. Models/Codex — Native Codex Provider

Section titled “1. Models/Codex — Native Codex Provider”
  • What changed: Added built-in Codex provider and plugin-level app-server harness. codex/gpt-* models use Codex-specific authentication, threads, model discovery, and compaction paths. openai/gpt-* retains the original OpenAI provider path.
  • Background: Previously, Codex models reused the OpenAI provider path, unable to leverage Codex’s native OAuth authentication, session thread management, and context compaction capabilities. Mixing two model sets in one provider caused authentication and feature conflicts.
  • Use cases: When configuring codex/gpt-4.1 or codex/gpt-5 as the model, it automatically uses the Codex authentication flow (OAuth) with native threading and compaction. Ideal for long coding sessions.
  • Notes: Requires configuring Codex OAuth scopes; existing openai/gpt-* configurations are unaffected; first use after upgrade requires completing OAuth authorization.
  • Evolution: OpenClaw initially supported only a single OpenAI provider → later added multi-provider architecture (OpenRouter, Anthropic, Ollama, etc.) → this version elevates Codex to a first-class independent provider.
  • Competitive landscape: Most similar products still treat Codex as an OpenAI variant without independent provider separation.
  • Future trends: Subsequent versions are expected to establish independent provider paths for more OpenAI sub-products (e.g., Sora, DALL·E).

2. Memory/Active Memory — Automatic Memory Recall Plugin

Section titled “2. Memory/Active Memory — Automatic Memory Recall Plugin”
  • What changed: Added optional Active Memory plugin that automatically runs a memory sub-agent before the main reply, pulling relevant preferences, context, and historical details. Supports message/recent/full context modes, /verbose real-time inspection, advanced prompt/thinking overrides, and optional transcript persistence.
  • Background: Previously, users had to manually say “remember this” or “search memory” to trigger the memory system. Useful context in daily conversations was being missed, rendering the memory system largely ineffective.
  • Use cases: When a user mentions “I’m going to Tokyo next week” in casual conversation, Active Memory automatically records and recalls it in subsequent conversations. No explicit commands needed. Configuration example: enable the plugin with context: "recent" mode, and the agent automatically queries recent relevant memories before each reply.
  • Notes: Adds latency to each reply (extra sub-agent call); increased token consumption; recommend starting with message mode (lightest) to evaluate before upgrading to full mode. Use /verbose to observe the recall process.
  • Evolution: OpenClaw memory system evolution: manual memory_search → MEMORY.md files → Dreaming (sleep-time memory consolidation) → this version’s Active Memory (real-time auto-recall).
  • Future trends: Active Memory + Dreaming will form a complete “remember-consolidate-recall” loop, with subsequent versions expected to optimize their synergy.

3. macOS/Talk — Local MLX Voice Provider

Section titled “3. macOS/Talk — Local MLX Voice Provider”
  • What changed: Added experimental local MLX voice provider supporting explicit provider selection, local audio playback, interruption handling, and system voice fallback.
  • Background: Talk Mode previously relied on cloud TTS services (e.g., ElevenLabs), suffering from high latency, privacy concerns, and network dependency. Apple Silicon chips on macOS are fully capable of running voice models locally.
  • Use cases: Using Talk Mode offline; privacy-sensitive conversation scenarios; automatic fallback to system voice when network is unstable.
  • Notes: macOS Apple Silicon (M1+) only; experimental feature — voice quality may not match cloud services; requires downloading MLX voice models.
  • Evolution: Talk Mode: cloud TTS only → this version adds local MLX option, evolving toward a hybrid architecture.

4. Tools/Video Generation — Seedance 2.0 Support

Section titled “4. Tools/Video Generation — Seedance 2.0 Support”
  • What changed: Added Seedance 2.0 model reference for the built-in fal provider, submitting duration, resolution, audio, seed and other provider-specific fields.
  • Use cases: Generate videos through OpenClaw using fal’s Seedance 2.0, with control over duration, resolution, audio, and other parameters.
  • Notes: Requires fal API key; video generation is asynchronous and time-consuming.

5. Microsoft Teams — Enhanced Message Actions

Section titled “5. Microsoft Teams — Enhanced Message Actions”
  • What changed: Added pin, unpin, read, react, and list reactions message actions.
  • Use cases: Agents can pin important messages, add emoji reactions, and mark as read.

6. QA/Matrix — Matrix Live Test Channel

Section titled “6. QA/Matrix — Matrix Live Test Channel”
  • What changed: Added live QA test channel based on disposable Matrix homeservers, covering threads, reactions, restarts, and allowlist behavior.
  • Use cases: Automated Matrix channel integration tests in CI/CD pipelines.

7. QA/Telegram — Telegram Live Test Channel

Section titled “7. QA/Telegram — Telegram Live Test Channel”
  • What changed: Added Telegram private group bot-to-bot test channel, hardened artifact handling, maintaining native Telegram command reply threads.

8. QA/Multipass — Virtual Machine Test Runner

Section titled “8. QA/Multipass — Virtual Machine Test Runner”
  • What changed: Added --runner multipass option allowing QA scenarios to run in disposable Linux VMs.

9. CLI/exec-policy — Execution Policy Management Command

Section titled “9. CLI/exec-policy — Execution Policy Management Command”
  • What changed: Added openclaw exec-policy command with show/preset/set subcommands for syncing tools.exec.* configuration with local exec approval files.
  • Use cases: openclaw exec-policy show to view current policy; openclaw exec-policy preset strict to quickly switch to strict mode.

10. Gateway/commands.list RPC

Section titled “10. Gateway/commands.list RPC”
  • What changed: Added commands.list RPC allowing remote gateway clients to discover runtime native commands, text commands, skill commands, and plugin commands.

11. Models/providers — Private Network Endpoint Support

Section titled “11. Models/providers — Private Network Endpoint Support”
  • What changed: Added models.providers.*.request.allowPrivateNetwork configuration allowing trusted self-hosted OpenAI-compatible endpoints.
  • Use cases: Connect to intranet-deployed vLLM, Ollama, and other OpenAI-compatible services.
  • Notes: Limited to model request surface only; does not affect other security policies. Must be enabled per provider.

12. Feishu — AI Agent Registration

Section titled “12. Feishu — AI Agent Registration”
  • What changed: Standardized request User-Agent, registering the bot as an AI Agent.

13. Matrix/Partial Streaming — MSC4357 Live Markers

Section titled “13. Matrix/Partial Streaming — MSC4357 Live Markers”
  • What changed: Added MSC4357 live markers for draft previews, supporting client-side typewriter animation rendering.

14. Control UI/Dreaming — Scene and Diary UI Improvements

Section titled “14. Control UI/Dreaming — Scene and Diary UI Improvements”
  • What changed: Simplified Scene and Diary interfaces, stabilized pending entry sorting.

15. Agents — GPT-5 Strict Execution Contract

Section titled “15. Agents — GPT-5 Strict Execution Contract”
  • What changed: Added optional strict-agentic embedded Pi execution contract where plan-only or filler turns continue executing until hitting a genuine blocker.
  • Use cases: Enable when using GPT-5 series models to ensure the agent keeps working until truly complete or blocked.
  • Notes: Opt-in feature requiring explicit enablement; may increase token consumption.

16. Agents/OpenAI — Codex Tool Compatibility

Section titled “16. Agents/OpenAI — Codex Tool Compatibility”
  • What changed: Added OpenAI/Codex tool schema compatibility and embedded run replay/liveness state.

17. Docs i18n — Documentation Translation Improvements

Section titled “17. Docs i18n — Documentation Translation Improvements”
  • What changed: Chunked translation of source documents, rejection of truncated tag output, recovery from terminated translation sessions.

Fixes

Section titled “Fixes”

1. Browser/Security — Browser Security Hardening (Major)

Section titled “1. Browser/Security — Browser Security Hardening (Major)”
  • What changed: Comprehensive hardening of browser and sandbox navigation defenses: strict SSRF defaults, hostname whitelist, interaction-driven redirects, subframes, CDP discovery, existing sessions, tab operations, noVNC, marker-span sanitization, Docker CDP origin scope enforcement.
  • Notes: ⚠️ May affect existing browser automation scripts after upgrade, especially those accessing intranet addresses.

2. Security/Tools — Tool Security Hardening (Major)

Section titled “2. Security/Tools — Tool Security Hardening (Major)”
  • What changed: Hardened exec preflight reads, host environment variable blocklist, node output boundaries, third-party media reads, profile change authorization, plugin install dependency scanning, tool hooks, token sanitization, oversized WebSocket frame handling.
  • Notes: ⚠️ Multiple security hardening measures may affect existing workflows. Full regression testing recommended.

3. OpenAI/Codex — Codex Integration Fixes

Section titled “3. OpenAI/Codex — Codex Integration Fixes”
  • What changed: Added required Codex OAuth scopes, improved provider/runtime error classification, stopped suggesting /elevated full when host exec is unavailable, maintained embedded run replay/liveness state.

4. CLI/WhatsApp Media Send Fix

Section titled “4. CLI/WhatsApp Media Send Fix”
  • What changed: Gateway mode --media sends now use the channel sendMedia path, fixing silent file drops when sending WhatsApp documents and attachments.

5. Microsoft Teams — Major Fixes

Section titled “5. Microsoft Teams — Major Fixes”
  • What changed: Fixed personal DM media download, Bot Framework conversations, OneDrive/SharePoint shared files, conversation IDs, Bot Framework audience tokens, SSO login callbacks, thread reply context injection, cron announcement delivery.
  • Notes: Teams users are strongly recommended to upgrade.

6. Gateway/Tailscale — Startup Order Optimization

Section titled “6. Gateway/Tailscale — Startup Order Optimization”
  • What changed: Tailscale exposure and update checks now execute before channel/plugin sidecar startup.

7. Gateway/Startup — Startup Stability

Section titled “7. Gateway/Startup — Startup Stability”
  • What changed: WebSocket RPC remains available during channel/plugin startup; chat.history delayed until sidecar completion; refreshed gateway methods after delayed plugin reload; upgrade flood protection.

8. WhatsApp — Reconnection Stability

OpenClaw Active Memory: Making AI Proactively Remember Who You Are

Apr 11, 2026
Vibe Sparking

The Problem

Section titled “The Problem”

Most AI memory systems are passive — they either wait for the user to say “remember this,” or rely on the main model to decide “maybe I should search my memory.” The problem: by the time the model realizes it should check, the best moment has already passed.

For example:

  • You say “what should I eat tonight?” and the AI doesn’t know you mentioned hating cilantro last week — it recommends a cilantro salad
  • You ask “help me book a flight” and the AI doesn’t know you prefer window seats and are an airline loyalty member
  • You say “weekend plans” and the AI doesn’t know you play badminton every Saturday

All this information exists in memory, but the main model simply never looked it up when generating its reply.

Active Memory’s approach is straightforward: before the main reply is generated, insert a lightweight memory sub-agent that searches relevant memories, injects the results into context, then lets the main model reply.

How It Works

Section titled “How It Works”

Key design decisions:

  1. Blocking — the main reply waits for it to complete, not async
  2. Hard timeout — 15 seconds by default; if it times out, it’s skipped without hanging
  3. Sub-agent limited to two tools — memory_search and memory_get only; it can’t go rogue
  4. Invisible to the user — injected as hidden system context; the user just sees a smarter reply
  5. Memory isolation per agent — each agent has its own SQLite database; no cross-contamination

Real-World Scenarios

Section titled “Real-World Scenarios”

Scenario 1: Personal Preferences Surface Automatically

Section titled “Scenario 1: Personal Preferences Surface Automatically”

The user previously mentioned “I like dark themes,” “I use Vim keybindings,” and “I hate YAML.”

Now the user says: “Help me configure my editor.”

Without Active Memory: AI gives generic configuration advice. With Active Memory: sub-agent finds preferences, main model directly provides dark theme + Vim keybinding config, skipping YAML format.

Scenario 2: Long-Term Project Context

Section titled “Scenario 2: Long-Term Project Context”

Last week, the user discussed “we’re migrating services from Docker Compose to K8s.”

Today the user says: “How should I update the deployment scripts?”

Without Active Memory: AI doesn’t know the migration context, might ask “what deployment method are you using?” With Active Memory: sub-agent finds the migration context, main model gives a solution based on the K8s migration.

Scenario 3: Personalization Across Multi-Agent Clusters

Section titled “Scenario 3: Personalization Across Multi-Agent Clusters”

We run 17 agents, each handling different domains (dev, ops, QA, product, etc.). Active Memory lets each agent remember user preferences and historical decisions relevant to its own domain, instead of starting from scratch every time.

Configuration

Section titled “Configuration”

Add to the plugins.entries section of openclaw.json:

Core Parameters

Section titled “Core Parameters”

queryMode — how much conversation the sub-agent sees:

ModeWhat It SeesLatencyBest For
messageLatest message onlyLowest (3-5s)Quick preference recall
recentLatest message + recent turnsMedium (~15s)Recommended starting point
fullFull conversation historyHighest (15s+)Deep context needed

promptStyle — how aggressively the sub-agent returns memories:

  • balanced: General default, recommended starting point
  • strict: Conservative, prefers returning nothing
  • recall-heavy: Aggressive recall, returns soft matches too
  • precision-heavy: Extremely conservative, only exact matches
  • preference-only: Focuses on preferences, habits, tastes
  • contextual: Emphasizes conversation continuity

allowedChatTypes — which chat types activate it:

  • direct: Private chats (recommended default)
  • group: Group chats
  • channel: Channels

Verification

Section titled “Verification”

Method 1: /verbose on

Section titled “Method 1: /verbose on”

Type /verbose on in any conversation session. Subsequent replies will include an Active Memory status line:

  • ok = running normally
  • 842ms = sub-agent duration
  • recent = query mode used
  • 34 chars = summary length injected

Method 2: /active-memory status

Section titled “Method 2: /active-memory status”

Check the Active Memory status for the current session:

Method 3: Gateway Logs

Section titled “Method 3: Gateway Logs”

With logging: true, you can see Active Memory run details in the gateway logs:

Method 4: Memory Health Check

Section titled “Method 4: Memory Health Check”

Verify the underlying memory system is working:

Method 5: Manual A/B Test

Section titled “Method 5: Manual A/B Test”
  1. Store a memory (mention a preference in conversation)
  2. Start a new session, /verbose on
  3. Ask a related but indirect question
  4. Check whether the Active Memory Debug line recalled that memory

Tuning Tips

Section titled “Tuning Tips”
  • Too noisy: Lower maxSummaryChars, or switch to strict / precision-heavy style
  • Too slow: Downgrade queryMode to message, shorten timeoutMs
  • No recall: Verify openclaw memory status --deep is healthy, confirm agent id is in the list
  • Debugging: Temporarily enable persistTranscripts: true to keep sub-agent transcripts (watch for file accumulation)

Our Deployment

Section titled “Our Deployment”
  • Instance: Local machine (OpenClaw 2026.4.10)
  • Scope: All 17 agents
  • Memory isolation: Each agent has its own SQLite database, no cross-contamination

Full Configuration

Section titled “Full Configuration”

Configuration Summary

Section titled “Configuration Summary”
ParameterValueNotes
agentsAll 17Every agent enabled
allowedChatTypesdirectPrivate chats only
queryModerecentLatest message + recent turns
promptStylebalancedGeneral balanced style
timeoutMs1500015-second hard timeout
maxSummaryChars220Summary cap at 220 chars
modelFallbackPolicydefault-remoteUse built-in remote default when no explicit model
persistTranscriptsfalseDon’t keep sub-agent transcripts
loggingtrueDebug logging on (during tuning)

Claude Code 2.1.98 Deep Dive: 8 New Features + 40+ Fixes Fully Analyzed

Apr 10, 2026
Vibe Sparking

Release date: April 2026 (extracted from CHANGELOG.md) Previous version: 2.1.97 | Analysis generated: 2026-04-10

Overview

Section titled “Overview”

2.1.98 is a heavyweight update containing 8 new features and 40+ fixes and improvements. Core themes:

  1. Enterprise Platform Support Enhancement — Google Vertex AI guided setup, Perforce integration
  2. Security Overhaul — Multiple Bash permission bypass vulnerabilities fixed (CVE-level)
  3. Stability Polish — Numerous edge case fixes for /resume, MCP, and permission systems
  4. Developer Experience Improvements — Monitor tool, Vim mode enhancements, OTEL tracing refinements

I. New Features In-Depth

Section titled “I. New Features In-Depth”

1.1 Google Vertex AI Interactive Configuration Wizard

Section titled “1.1 Google Vertex AI Interactive Configuration Wizard”

Change: After selecting “3rd-party platform” on the login screen, a complete GCP guided flow is now available — authentication, project/region selection, credential verification, and model binding all in one step.

Background: Previously, Vertex AI configuration required manually setting multiple environment variables (ANTHROPIC_VERTEX_PROJECT_ID, CLOUD_ML_REGION, etc.), creating a high barrier for users unfamiliar with GCP, with configuration errors difficult to diagnose.

Use Cases:

  • Enterprise users deploying Claude Code on GCP for the first time
  • New team members quickly onboarding without reading configuration docs
  • Switching between multiple projects/regions directly through the wizard

Notes:

  • Requires gcloud CLI installed locally with basic authentication completed
  • Region selection affects latency and model availability (some models only available in regions like us-east5)
  • Model pinning writes to local config; switching requires re-running the wizard

Comparison:

  • Codex CLI: Relies on OpenAI API key, no platform wizard, relatively simpler config
  • Gemini CLI: Native Google product, works after gcloud auth, no additional config needed
  • Claude Code’s move closes the experience gap with Gemini CLI in the GCP ecosystem

Historical Context: 2.1.94 added Bedrock Mantle support, 2.1.97 fixed Bedrock SigV4 authentication issues. The Vertex AI wizard is a continuation of the cloud platform integration strategy.

1.2 Perforce Mode (CLAUDE_CODE_PERFORCE_MODE)

Section titled “1.2 Perforce Mode (CLAUDE_CODE_PERFORCE_MODE)”

Change: When this environment variable is set, Edit/Write/NotebookEdit will error and prompt p4 edit when encountering read-only files, rather than silently overwriting.

Background: Large gaming, chip design, and other industries widely use Perforce (P4) for version control. P4’s workflow is fundamentally different from Git — files are read-only by default and must be checked out (p4 edit) before modification. AI coding tools directly overwriting read-only files can cause lost changes and workspace state corruption.

Use Cases:

  • Game studios using Unreal Engine + P4 for large projects
  • Chip RTL code repositories (typically 100GB+ P4 depots)
  • Any hybrid Git + P4 workflow

Notes:

  • Requires setting CLAUDE_CODE_PERFORCE_MODE=1 in shell profile or project .env
  • Currently only blocks writes and prompts; doesn’t auto-execute p4 edit (likely a security consideration)
  • Works best with P4’s .p4config

Comparison:

  • Codex CLI / Gemini CLI: No Perforce support; P4 users must handle it themselves
  • Claude Code is the first AI coding tool with native Perforce workflow support — a differentiator in the enterprise market

Future Evolution: Subsequent versions may add automatic p4 edit capability (requiring permission confirmation) and P4 changelist integration.

1.3 Monitor Tool — Background Script Event Stream

Section titled “1.3 Monitor Tool — Background Script Event Stream”

Change: New Monitor tool for streaming events from background scripts.

Background: Claude Code already supports running scripts in the background (subagents, long builds, etc.), but previously lacked real-time monitoring capabilities — you could only wait for completion or poll logs.

Use Cases:

  • Monitoring progress of long-running test suites
  • Watching real-time output of background build/deploy scripts
  • Debugging anomalies during subagent execution

Notes:

  • Works better in combination with the 2.1.98 fix for “background subagent failures not reporting partial progress”
  • Event stream format may change across versions

Comparison:

  • Codex CLI: Supports --stream output but no standalone monitoring tool
  • Gemini CLI: No background task monitoring capability yet

1.4 Subprocess Sandbox Hardening (PID Namespace Isolation)

Section titled “1.4 Subprocess Sandbox Hardening (PID Namespace Isolation)”

Change:

  • On Linux, setting CLAUDE_CODE_SUBPROCESS_ENV_SCRUB enables PID namespace isolation
  • New CLAUDE_CODE_SCRIPT_CAPS limits per-session script invocation count

Background: As Claude Code is used in more sensitive environments (production servers, CI/CD), subprocess isolation needs grow stronger. PID namespaces prevent subprocesses from seeing or manipulating other processes on the host.

Use Cases:

  • Restricting Claude Code subprocess permissions in CI/CD pipelines
  • Security isolation in multi-tenant environments
  • Limiting script execution count per session to prevent runaway loops

Notes:

  • PID namespace is Linux-only (macOS doesn’t support this kernel feature)
  • Requires root or CAP_SYS_ADMIN to create namespaces
  • CLAUDE_CODE_SCRIPT_CAPS upper limit needs tuning based on workload

Comparison:

  • Codex CLI: Uses Docker containers for isolation — coarser grained but more mature
  • Gemini CLI: No explicit sandbox mechanism yet
  • Claude Code’s approach is lighter weight, suitable for environments where Docker isn’t available

1.5 Print Mode Cross-User Cache Optimization

Section titled “1.5 Print Mode Cross-User Cache Optimization”

Change: --exclude-dynamic-system-prompt-sections flag excludes dynamic system prompt sections in print mode.

Background: Claude Code’s print mode is used for batch/automation scenarios. Dynamic parts of system prompts (usernames, timestamps, etc.) prevent prompt cache sharing across users, wasting tokens.

Use Cases:

  • Enterprise batch code review pipelines
  • Reducing API costs in multi-user shared CI services
  • Prompt cache hit rate optimization

Notes:

  • Excluded sections may contain useful context — trade-offs required
  • Only affects print mode; interactive mode unaffected

1.6 Git Worktree Status Recognition

Section titled “1.6 Git Worktree Status Recognition”

Change: Status line JSON now includes workspace.git_worktree field.

Background: Git worktree allows multiple working directories for the same repository, commonly used for parallel development/code review. Claude Code previously couldn’t distinguish between main and linked worktrees, potentially causing path confusion.

Use Cases:

  • Parallel PR processing using worktrees
  • Correct context identification when running Claude Code in a worktree
  • Custom status line scripts adjusting behavior based on worktree status

Notes: 2.1.97 initially added this field; 2.1.98 ensures it’s correctly set in all scenarios.

1.7 OTEL Tracing — TRACEPARENT Propagation

Section titled “1.7 OTEL Tracing — TRACEPARENT Propagation”

Change: Bash subprocesses automatically inherit the W3C TRACEPARENT environment variable.

Background: With OpenTelemetry tracing enabled, subprocess spans couldn’t properly attach to Claude Code’s trace tree, breaking distributed tracing chains.

Use Cases:

  • Enterprise observability platform integration (Datadog, Honeycomb, Jaeger)
  • Debugging cross-process performance bottlenecks
  • Auditing all subprocess call chains triggered by Claude Code

1.8 LSP clientInfo Identification

Section titled “1.8 LSP clientInfo Identification”

Change: Claude Code now identifies itself via the clientInfo field in LSP initialize requests.

Background: Language servers (LSP) couldn’t distinguish between requests from Claude Code and other editors, making targeted optimization or debugging difficult.

Use Cases:

  • LSP servers adjusting behavior based on client type
  • Quick source identification when debugging LSP interaction issues

II. Security Fixes (Critical)

Section titled “II. Security Fixes (Critical)”

This version fixes multiple severe permission bypass vulnerabilities — the most critical part of this update.

2.1 Bash Tool Backslash Escape Bypass (Severe)

Section titled “2.1 Bash Tool Backslash Escape Bypass (Severe)”

Issue: Backslash-escaped flags could be auto-approved as “read-only” operations while actually executing arbitrary code.

Impact: Attackers (or malicious prompts) could craft commands with backslashes to bypass permission checks, executing dangerous operations in auto mode.

Fix: Normalize escape characters before permission matching.

2.2 Compound Command Bypass of Forced Permission Prompts

Section titled “2.2 Compound Command Bypass of Forced Permission Prompts”

Issue: Pipes, &&, ;, and other compound commands could bypass auto and bypass-permissions mode security checks.

Impact: Even with strict permission rules configured, dangerous parts within compound commands could be silently executed.

2.3 Environment Variable Prefix Bypass

Section titled “2.3 Environment Variable Prefix Bypass”

Issue: Commands in ENV_VAR=value dangerous_command format, if ENV_VAR wasn’t in the known safe list, wouldn’t trigger permission prompts.

Fix: Now only known safe variables like LANG, TZ, NO_COLOR are exempt from prompts.

2.4 /dev/tcp and /dev/udp Redirections

Section titled “2.4 /dev/tcp and /dev/udp Redirections”

Issue: Redirections to /dev/tcp/... or /dev/udp/... were auto-allowed, enabling data exfiltration.

Fix: Such redirections now force a prompt.

2.5 Other Permission-Related Fixes

Section titled “2.5 Other Permission-Related Fixes”
  • --dangerously-skip-permissions silently downgraded to accept-edits after writing to protected paths
  • Admin-removed managed-settings rules remained effective until restart
  • additionalDirectories changes didn’t take effect in real-time
  • Wildcard rules Bash(cmd:*) didn’t match commands with extra spaces
  • Deny rules downgraded in pipe commands containing cd
  • grep -f / rg -f reading files outside working directory without prompting
  • JS prototype property names (e.g., toString) causing settings.json to be ignored

Overall Assessment: This is a comprehensive security audit fix. Users of auto mode or bypass-permissions should upgrade immediately.

Comparison:

  • Codex CLI: Uses Docker sandbox; different permission model; these bypasses don’t apply
  • Gemini CLI: Simpler permission system; smaller attack surface but also fewer features

III. Stability & Experience Fixes

Section titled “III. Stability & Experience Fixes”

3.1 Streaming Response & Retry

Section titled “3.1 Streaming Response & Retry”
  • Streaming response timeout now falls back to non-streaming mode (instead of failing outright)
  • Exponential backoff fix for 429 retries: previously burned through all retries within 13 seconds when Retry-After was small
  • 2.1.97 initially fixed this; 2.1.98 further refines it

3.2 Comprehensive /resume Fixes

Section titled “3.2 Comprehensive /resume Fixes”
  • --resume <name> opened as non-editable
  • Filter refresh clearing search state
  • Empty list swallowing arrow keys
  • Cross-project expiration issues
  • Task status text replacing conversation summaries
  • Added project/worktree/branch name filter indicators

3.3 Terminal Compatibility

Section titled “3.3 Terminal Compatibility”
  • Uppercase letters becoming lowercase under kitty keyboard protocol (xterm, VS Code terminal)
  • macOS text replacement deleting trigger words
  • Fullscreen mode MCP tool result hover crash
  • URL copy inserting line break spaces

3.4 MCP-Related

Section titled “3.4 MCP-Related”
  • OAuth authServerMetadataUrl not taking effect for token refresh after restart
  • _meta["anthropic/maxResultSizeChars"] not bypassing token persistence layer

3.5 Permission System Real-Time Updates

Section titled “3.5 Permission System Real-Time Updates”
  • permissions.additionalDirectories changes take effect immediately
  • Removing directories no longer erroneously revokes same-named directories passed via --add-dir
  • Managed-settings rule removal takes effect immediately

IV. Improvements

Section titled “IV. Improvements”

4.1 /agents Tab Layout

Section titled “4.1 /agents Tab Layout”

New Running tab shows active subagents; Library tab adds “Run agent” and “View instances” actions.

4.2 Vim Mode Enhancements

Section titled “4.2 Vim Mode Enhancements”

NORMAL mode j/k navigates history; reaching input boundary selects footer pill.

4.3 Accept Edits Mode Intelligence

Section titled “4.3 Accept Edits Mode Intelligence”

File system commands with safe environment variable prefixes or process wrappers (e.g., LANG=C rm foo, timeout 5 mkdir out) auto-approved.

4.4 Hook Error Diagnostics

Section titled “4.4 Hook Error Diagnostics”

Hook errors in transcripts now include first line of stderr — self-diagnosable without --debug.

4.5 DISABLE_COMPACT Refinement

Section titled “4.5 DISABLE_COMPACT Refinement”

With DISABLE_COMPACT set, /compact prompt no longer displayed; CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_CONTEXT_TOKENS correctly respects this setting.

V. Trend Analysis

Section titled “V. Trend Analysis”

5.1 Accelerating Enterprise Focus

Section titled “5.1 Accelerating Enterprise Focus”

Vertex AI wizard, Perforce support, PID isolation, OTEL tracing — nearly all 2.1.98 new features target enterprise users. Claude Code is evolving from “developer tool” to “enterprise development platform.”

5.2 Security Maturity Leap

Section titled “5.2 Security Maturity Leap”

Fixing 10+ permission bypass issues at once indicates Anthropic conducted a systematic security audit. This is the necessary path for AI coding tools moving toward production environments. Expect subsequent versions to continue tightening the permission model.

5.3 Multi-Platform Ecosystem

Section titled “5.3 Multi-Platform Ecosystem”

From AWS Bedrock to GCP Vertex AI, Claude Code is building a multi-cloud support matrix. Compared to Codex CLI (OpenAI only) and Gemini CLI (Google only), this is a unique competitive advantage.

5.4 SubAgent System Maturation

Section titled “5.4 SubAgent System Maturation”

Monitor tool, subagent error reporting, worktree cleanup fixes — multi-agent architecture continues to evolve. Claude Code is becoming an agent orchestration platform.

VI. Upgrade Recommendations

Section titled “VI. Upgrade Recommendations”
  • Auto/bypass-permissions mode users: Upgrade immediately (security fixes)
  • GCP Vertex AI users: Recommended upgrade (new wizard dramatically lowers config barrier)
  • Perforce users: Recommended upgrade (first native support)
  • General users: Suggested upgrade (terminal compatibility and stability improvements)

Notes: 2.1.97 initially added this field; 2.1.98 ensures it’s correctly set in all scenarios.

1.7 OTEL Tracing — TRACEPARENT Propagation

Section titled “1.7 OTEL Tracing — TRACEPARENT Propagation”

What changed: Bash subprocesses now automatically inherit the W3C TRACEPARENT environment variable.

Background: When OpenTelemetry tracing was enabled, subprocess spans couldn’t properly attach to Claude Code’s trace tree, causing broken distributed traces.

Use cases:

  • Enterprise observability platform integration (Datadog, Honeycomb, Jaeger)
  • Debugging cross-process performance bottlenecks
  • Auditing all subprocess call chains triggered by Claude Code

1.8 LSP clientInfo Identification

Section titled “1.8 LSP clientInfo Identification”

What changed: Claude Code now identifies itself through the clientInfo field in LSP initialize requests.

Background: Language servers (LSP) couldn’t distinguish between requests from Claude Code and other editors, making it difficult to apply targeted optimizations or debugging.

Use cases:

  • LSP servers adjusting behavior based on client type
  • Quickly identifying the source when debugging LSP interaction issues

II. Security Fixes (Critical)

Section titled “II. Security Fixes (Critical)”

This release fixes multiple serious permission bypass vulnerabilities — the most critical part of this update.

2.1 Bash Tool Backslash Escape Bypass (Critical)

Section titled “2.1 Bash Tool Backslash Escape Bypass (Critical)”

Issue: Backslash-escaped flags could be auto-approved as “read-only” operations while actually executing arbitrary code.

Impact: An attacker (or malicious prompt) could craft commands with backslashes to bypass permission checks and execute dangerous operations in auto mode.

Fix: Escape characters are now normalized before permission matching.

2.2 Compound Command Bypass of Forced Permission Prompts

Section titled “2.2 Compound Command Bypass of Forced Permission Prompts”

Issue: Compound commands using pipes, &&, ;, etc. could bypass security checks in both auto and bypass-permissions modes.

Impact: Even with strict permission rules configured, dangerous parts of compound commands could be silently executed.

2.3 Environment Variable Prefix Bypass

Section titled “2.3 Environment Variable Prefix Bypass”

Issue: Commands in the format ENV_VAR=value dangerous_command would not trigger a permission prompt if ENV_VAR wasn’t on the known safe list.

Fix: Only known safe variables like LANG, TZ, NO_COLOR are now exempt from prompting.

2.4 /dev/tcp and /dev/udp Redirects

Section titled “2.4 /dev/tcp and /dev/udp Redirects”

Issue: Redirects to /dev/tcp/... or /dev/udp/... were automatically allowed and could be used for data exfiltration.

Fix: Such redirects now force a permission prompt.

2.5 Other Permission-Related Fixes

Section titled “2.5 Other Permission-Related Fixes”
  • --dangerously-skip-permissions silently downgraded to accept-edits after writing to protected paths
  • Admin-removed managed-settings rules remained effective until restart
  • additionalDirectories changes didn’t take effect in real time
  • Wildcard rules like Bash(cmd:*) didn’t match commands with extra spaces
  • Deny rules were downgraded in piped commands containing cd
  • grep -f / rg -f reading files outside the working directory didn’t trigger a prompt
  • JS prototype property names (e.g., toString) caused settings.json to be ignored

Overall assessment: This is a comprehensive security audit fix. Users running auto mode or bypass-permissions should upgrade immediately.

Comparison with similar products:

  • Codex CLI: Uses Docker sandbox with a different permission model; these bypasses don’t apply
  • Gemini CLI: Simpler permissions system with a smaller attack surface but also fewer features

III. Stability and Experience Fixes

Section titled “III. Stability and Experience Fixes”

3.1 Streaming Responses and Retries

Section titled “3.1 Streaming Responses and Retries”
  • Streaming responses now fall back to non-streaming mode after timeout (instead of failing outright)
  • Exponential backoff fix for 429 retries: previously, small Retry-After values burned through all retries within 13 seconds
  • 2.1.97 initially fixed this issue; 2.1.98 further refines it

3.2 Comprehensive /resume Fixes

Section titled “3.2 Comprehensive /resume Fixes”
  • --resume <name> opened as non-editable
  • Filter refresh cleared search state
  • Empty list swallowed arrow keys
  • Cross-project expiration issues
  • Task status text replaced conversation summaries
  • Added project/worktree/branch name filter indicators

3.3 Terminal Compatibility

Section titled “3.3 Terminal Compatibility”
  • Uppercase letters converted to lowercase under kitty keyboard protocol (xterm, VS Code terminal)
  • macOS text replacement deleted trigger words
  • Full-screen mode MCP tool result hover crash
  • URL copy inserting line break spaces

3.4 MCP-Related

Section titled “3.4 MCP-Related”
  • OAuth authServerMetadataUrl not working during token refresh after restart
  • _meta["anthropic/maxResultSizeChars"] not bypassing the token persistence layer

3.5 Permissions System Real-Time Updates

Section titled “3.5 Permissions System Real-Time Updates”
  • permissions.additionalDirectories changes now take effect immediately
  • Removing a directory no longer incorrectly revokes a same-named directory passed via --add-dir
  • Managed-settings rules take effect immediately after removal

IV. Improvements

Section titled “IV. Improvements”

4.1 /agents Tab Layout

Section titled “4.1 /agents Tab Layout”

New Running tab showing active subagents; Library tab adds “Run agent” and “View instances” actions.

4.2 Vim Mode Enhancements

Section titled “4.2 Vim Mode Enhancements”

NORMAL mode j/k navigates history, selecting the footer pill when reaching input boundaries.

4.3 Smarter Accept Edits Mode

Section titled “4.3 Smarter Accept Edits Mode”

Filesystem commands with safe environment variable prefixes or process wrappers (e.g., LANG=C rm foo, timeout 5 mkdir out) are now auto-approved.

4.4 Hook Error Diagnostics

Section titled “4.4 Hook Error Diagnostics”

Hook errors in transcripts now include the first line of stderr, enabling self-diagnosis without --debug.

4.5 DISABLE_COMPACT Refinements

Section titled “4.5 DISABLE_COMPACT Refinements”

When DISABLE_COMPACT is set, /compact prompts no longer appear, and CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_CONTEXT_TOKENS correctly respects this setting.

Section titled “5.1 Accelerating Enterprise Focus”

Vertex AI wizard, Perforce support, PID isolation, OTEL tracing — nearly all new features in 2.1.98 target enterprise users. Claude Code is evolving from a “developer tool” into an “enterprise development platform.”

Fixing 10+ permission bypass issues at once indicates Anthropic conducted a systematic security audit. This is a necessary step for AI coding tools moving into production environments. Expect continued tightening of the permission model in future releases.

From AWS Bedrock to GCP Vertex AI, Claude Code is building a multi-cloud support matrix. Compared to Codex CLI (OpenAI only) and Gemini CLI (Google only), this is a unique competitive advantage.

Claude Code 2.1.97 Deep Dive: 50+ Changes Fully Analyzed

Apr 9, 2026
Vibe Sparking

Release date: 2026-04-09 Changes: 50+

Version Overview

Section titled “Version Overview”

2.1.97 is a major maintenance and feature release containing approximately 50+ changes, covering new features, permission systems, MCP, session recovery, NO_FLICKER rendering, enterprise integration, and numerous reliability fixes. The overall signal is clear: this version isn’t about single-point innovation, but about polishing Claude Code’s core execution surface to be more stable and better suited for high-frequency real-world development usage.

I. New Features

Section titled “I. New Features”

1. Focus View Toggle (Ctrl+O) in NO_FLICKER Mode

Section titled “1. Focus View Toggle (Ctrl+O) in NO_FLICKER Mode”

Change Content

  • Added Focus View in NO_FLICKER mode
  • Display includes: user prompt, one-line summary of tool calls, edit diffstats, final response

Problem Background

  • NO_FLICKER mode solves the traditional terminal flickering problem, but introduces another issue: information hierarchy can become mixed in long sessions
  • Users often don’t want to see all raw tool outputs, but want to quickly understand “what I asked, what it did, how much was changed, what was the final answer”

Use Cases

  • Quick review after long refactoring tasks
  • Recapping an agent’s work process to colleagues
  • Reviewing results after numerous Bash, Read, Edit, Write tool calls
  • Need to quickly locate operation summaries for failed tasks

Example

  • User asks Claude to refactor auth module
  • Focus View only shows:
    • prompt: “Refactor auth to JWT middleware”
    • tool summary: Read 4 files, Edit 3 files, Bash npm test
    • diffstats: +84 -27
    • final response: “JWT middleware refactor completed, tests pass”

Notes

  • Only available in NO_FLICKER mode
  • Better suited for summary browsing, not for replacing full step-by-step debugging
  • If you need to see detailed shell output step by step, still return to full view

Historical Context

  • 2.1.89 introduced CLAUDE_CODE_NO_FLICKER=1
  • 2.1.90 to 2.1.97 continuously fixed multiple NO_FLICKER rendering, scrolling, copying, and shortcut issues
  • This addition of Focus View indicates NO_FLICKER is transitioning from “experimental rendering layer” to “usable workflow interface” stage

Competitor Comparison

  • Codex CLI
    • Typically more focused on raw streaming output
    • Lacks this hierarchical focus review view
  • Gemini CLI
    • Emphasizes structured output and extension ecosystem
    • Also lacks this session summary view oriented toward long coding sessions

Future Trend Prediction

  • More view toggles may appear later, such as diff-only, tools-only, errors-only
  • Claude Code may gradually evolve terminal sessions into a “navigable work record interface” rather than just a text stream

2. refreshInterval Status Line Setting

Section titled “2. refreshInterval Status Line Setting”

Change Content

  • Added refreshInterval status bar setting
  • Allows status bar commands to automatically rerun every N seconds

Problem Background

  • Previously, status bar was more like static information or low-frequency updates
  • For real-time changing information like current branch status, task queues, backend service health status, single render wasn’t enough

Use Cases

  • Real-time display of git branch, worktree, repo status
  • Real-time display of local dev server, test watcher, CI status
  • Display current machine status or session information during remote development

Example

  • Execute a status command every 5 seconds, showing:
    • Current branch
    • Current worktree
    • Whether background tests pass
    • Whether current directory has uncommitted changes

Notes

  • Too frequent refreshing increases performance overhead
  • Status bar commands should be lightweight to avoid causing lag
  • Be especially careful with heavy git/status commands in large monorepos

Historical Context

  • 2.1.94 added richer status/UI information management
  • 2.1.97 simultaneously added workspace.git_worktree, these two changes are clearly complementary

Competitor Comparison

  • Codex CLI status UI is relatively simple, lacking this obvious customizable status bar refresh mechanism
  • Gemini CLI has footer/UI improvements, but support for “custom status command timed refresh” isn’t as development-workflow oriented as Claude Code

Future Trend Prediction

  • Status bar may later support more dynamic contexts like token usage, agent count, task status, network status
  • Long-term may evolve into customizable development cockpit

3. workspace.git_worktree Injected into Status Bar JSON

Section titled “3. workspace.git_worktree Injected into Status Bar JSON”

Change Content

  • When current directory is in a linked git worktree, status bar JSON input adds workspace.git_worktree

Problem Background

  • Git worktree is high-frequency advanced development usage, especially suitable for parallel bug fixing, parallel feature development, parallel agent execution
  • Many tools only recognize repo root, not current worktree identity, leading to misleading status

Use Cases

  • Opening multiple worktrees in one repository for different branch tasks
  • One Claude main session + multiple subagents each bound to different worktrees
  • Quickly confirm through status bar that you’re not in main working directory but in some linked worktree

Example

  • Main repository at /repo
  • Current directory at /repo-feature-auth
  • Status bar can display worktree=feature-auth

Notes

  • Only has value in linked worktree scenarios
  • Custom status scripts need to handle empty field cases

Historical Context

  • 2.1.92 improved --resume to directly restore sessions from other worktrees in same repo
  • This version fixes subagent worktree isolation leaking to parent Bash tool
  • Indicates Claude Code is systematically completing worktree-first development experience

Competitor Comparison

  • Codex CLI worktree experience is currently more “you handle paths yourself”
  • Gemini CLI also lacks this explicit worktree status exposure capability

Future Trend Prediction

  • May later add branch, dirty state, ahead/behind, repo root identity fields
  • Worktree may become default isolation unit for multi-agent parallel programming

4. Added ● N running Indicator in /agents

Section titled “4. Added ● N running Indicator in /agents”

Change Content

  • In /agents list, when an agent type has active subagent instances, displays ● N running

Problem Background

  • Claude Code’s subagent/agent system is gradually strengthening, but observability has been a barrier
  • Users often don’t know which agents are running, whether they’re dead or busy

Use Cases

  • Multiple subagents concurrently executing code search, testing, documentation summarization
  • Checking if an agent type already has instances running to avoid duplicate launches
  • Debugging agent stuck issues

Example

  • In /agents output see:
    • code-research ● 2 running
    • refactor-helper ● 1 running
    • docs-agent

Notes

  • This is visibility enhancement, doesn’t mean agent orchestration logic itself changed
  • If agent instance state synchronization is delayed, may still need to combine with specific session judgment

Historical Context

  • 2.1.89 added named subagents to @ mention typeahead
  • 2.1.92 fixed tmux changes causing permanent subagent spawning failure
  • This version also fixes subagent cwd/worktree leakage

Competitor Comparison

  • Codex CLI current mainstream usage is still more single-agent oriented
  • Gemini CLI has rich extension ecosystem, but native multi-subagent interaction management isn’t as deep as Claude Code

Future Trend Prediction

  • May later add agent CPU/time/token visualization
  • May eventually form interactive panel similar to “job manager / task supervisor”

5. Cedar Policy File Syntax Highlighting

Section titled “5. Cedar Policy File Syntax Highlighting”

Change Content

  • Added syntax highlighting for .cedar and .cedarpolicy files

Problem Background

  • Cedar is increasingly important DSL in permission policy domain, especially growing in cloud permissions, fine-grained authorization, and policy-as-code
  • Lack of syntax highlighting significantly reduces readability

Use Cases

  • Combined with continuous permission system hardening, has flavor of evolving toward enterprise security development tools

II. Permission & Security Fixes

Section titled “II. Permission & Security Fixes”

6. Fixed --dangerously-skip-permissions Silent Downgrade Issue

Section titled “6. Fixed --dangerously-skip-permissions Silent Downgrade Issue”

Problem Background

  • This parameter, as the name suggests, is very dangerous, meaning skip permission restrictions
  • Previously, after approving one write operation to protected path, would be silently downgraded to accept-edits mode
  • Worst part: users didn’t know it changed

Why This is Serious Problem

  • In automated scripts or controlled CI, this “I thought still fully allowed, actually already semi-allowed” behavior creates unpredictability
  • Not transparent security-wise, unreliable engineering-wise

Use Cases

  • Unattended automatic environment modifications
  • Large-scale migrations in trusted local sandboxes

Notes

  • Even after fix, not recommended for daily use of this parameter
  • Only use when you completely trust environment, explicitly accept risks

Historical Context

  • 2.1.90 started continuously strengthening permission model
  • Multiple permission fixes this version indicate permission system moving from “usable” to “predictable and consistent”

Competitor Comparison

  • Codex CLI has clearer full-auto/semi-auto mode distinction, but usually more straightforward in explainability
  • Gemini CLI YOLO/accept-edits is also clear
  • Claude Code fixing “mode semantic instability” problem is fundamentally crucial

7. Bash Tool Permission Hardening

Section titled “7. Bash Tool Permission Hardening”

Change Content

  • Strengthened env-var prefix checking
  • Strengthened network redirection related checking
  • Simultaneously reduced false positives for common commands

Problem Background

  • Bash permission control is difficult because shell syntax is too complex
  • Attacks or bypasses often hide in:
    • Environment variable prefixes
    • Wrapper commands
    • Redirections
    • Compound commands

Typical Problem Scenarios

  • FOO=bar curl ...
  • LANG=C rm foo
  • timeout 5 mkdir out
  • cmd > /sensitive/path

This Fix Value

  • On one hand plugging vulnerabilities, on other hand reducing false positives
  • Shows team isn’t just tightening, but balancing “high security + low friction”

Notes

  • Shell permission systems always have edge cases
  • High-risk environments should still rely on outer sandbox, not just trust CLI’s own rules

Historical Context

  • 2.1.89 fixed hook if condition failing to match env prefixes and compound commands
  • 2.1.90 strengthened PowerShell permission checking
  • 2.1.97 further improved Bash permission checking

Competitor Comparison

  • Codex CLI tends to use more outer isolation and mode control
  • Gemini CLI yolo/shell/accept-edits model easier to understand, but granularity may not be as high as Claude Code

Future Trend Prediction

  • May later introduce more formal shell command normalization layer
  • Long-term may develop into declarative command risk classification system

8. Permission Rule Name Colliding with JS Prototype Properties Causing settings.json to be Ignored

Section titled “8. Permission Rule Name Colliding with JS Prototype Properties Causing settings.json to be Ignored”

Problem Background

  • If permission rule name is JavaScript prototype property name like toString, settings.json would be silently ignored

Root Cause

  • Typical JS object key handling error
  • When using plain objects as maps, prototype pollution or prototype key collision is classic pitfall

Use Cases

  • When enterprises/teams define permission rule names themselves, accidentally hitting these reserved properties

Why Important

  • Worst part is “silent ignore”
  • Users think rules are effective, but entire permission configuration may not be effective

Notes

  • This type of problem exposes configuration system robustness was insufficient
  • For enterprise administrators, this silent failure is much more dangerous than explicit errors

Competitor Comparison

  • This is implementation layer quality issue, not feature comparison point
  • But from product maturity perspective, Claude Code is paying down this enterprise-level edge reliability debt

9. Managed-settings Allow Rules Still Effective After Removal Until Restart

Section titled “9. Managed-settings Allow Rules Still Effective After Removal Until Restart”

Problem Background

  • Administrator remotely removed allow rules, but old rules continued effective in local process until restart

Impact

  • Management policies cannot be immediately revoked
  • In security governance, this is serious consistency problem

Use Cases

  • Enterprise administrator urgently revoking access to certain directory, command, or network capability

Notes

  • Immediate effectiveness is very important for enterprises
  • Once this type of problem exists, significantly weakens managed settings credibility

Historical Context

  • 2.1.92 added forceRemoteSettingsRefresh, emphasizing fail-closed semantics
  • This version fixes hot update not revoking problem, belongs to same governance chain completion

10. permissions.additionalDirectories Mid-session Modifications Not Effective

Section titled “10. permissions.additionalDirectories Mid-session Modifications Not Effective”

Problem Background

  • Additional allowed directories in settings not applied when modified during session runtime

Scenario

  • Temporarily opening sibling repo, shared config directory, external script directory during development

Impact

  • Users modify configuration but still need to restart session, breaking flow

11. Error Removing --add-dir Permissions When Removing Directory from additionalDirectories

Section titled “11. Error Removing --add-dir Permissions When Removing Directory from additionalDirectories”

Problem Background

  • Directory exists both through settings and --add-dir
  • After removing from settings, should still retain access rights from --add-dir
  • Previously both were revoked together

Root Cause

  • Multi-source permission merging logic error
  • Didn’t correctly do source-aware permission bookkeeping

Why Important

  • Multi-layer permission sources is enterprise environment norm
  • Permission system must support “precise addition/removal by source”, cannot brutally override

12. MCP HTTP/SSE Reconnection Memory Leak, ~50MB/Hour

Section titled “12. MCP HTTP/SSE Reconnection Memory Leak, ~50MB/Hour”

Problem Background

  • MCP heavily relies on HTTP/SSE long connections
  • When server repeatedly reconnects, buffers not released
  • Long sessions or unstable network environments steadily consume memory

Use Cases

  • Long-term connections to databases, browsers, remote knowledge bases, internal tool MCP servers
  • Environments with average network quality where server actively disconnects and reconnects

Example

  • 8 hours workday, if leaking 50MB/hour, that’s 400MB
  • Combined with other caches and transcript, quickly becomes noticeable performance issue

Notes

  • This is typical stability pain point for “long-running agent tools”
  • Significantly impacts those using Claude Code as all-day development partner

Historical Context

  • 2.1.90 fixed SSE transport quadratic complexity issue for large streamed frames
  • 2.1.92 fixed plugin MCP stuck connecting
  • 2.1.97 fixes buffer unreleased, indicating MCP communication stack still being polished

Competitor Comparison

  • Codex CLI native MCP ecosystem not as heavy as Claude Code
  • Gemini CLI also pushing MCP/extensions, but Claude Code deeper in real IDE-like agent integration, so these problems exposed earlier

Future Trend Prediction

  • MCP will increasingly become “AI tool bus”
  • Stability, reconnection, backpressure, memory recycling will become next phase core engineering competition points

13. MCP OAuth oauth.authServerMetadataUrl Token Refresh Not Effective After Restart

Section titled “13. MCP OAuth oauth.authServerMetadataUrl Token Refresh Not Effective After Restart”

Problem Background

  • Enterprise identity providers like ADFS rely on this metadata URL
  • Token refresh after restart didn’t correctly honor this setting

Use Cases

  • Enterprise SSO login
  • Self-hosted OAuth or ADFS-compatible MCP services

Impact

  • Initial login may succeed, subsequent refreshes fail
  • Causes most annoying enterprise problem: “seems usable, suddenly breaks after some time”

Notes

  • These problems typically only appear heavily in enterprise environments, high compliance environments
  • Ordinary individual users may not encounter, but once encountered almost judged as unusable

IV. Rate Limit & API Reliability

Section titled “IV. Rate Limit & API Reliability”

14. Fixed 429 Retry Too Fast Exhaustion Problem

Section titled “14. Fixed 429 Retry Too Fast Exhaustion Problem”

Problem Background

  • Server returns small Retry-After
  • Client uses this small value as primary basis, causing too fast retries
  • All retries exhausted in about 13 seconds

Why This is Bad Experience

  • Users encounter recoverable rate limiting, but due to overly aggressive client strategy, directly becomes failure
  • Makes people mistakenly think “service completely unavailable”

Fix Content

  • Exponential backoff now applied as minimum lower bound
  • Even if server gives small Retry-After, won’t blindly densely retry

Use Cases

  • API temporary congestion
  • Enterprise proxy layer, Cloudflare, gateway layer rate limiting
  • High concurrency subagents triggering burst

Historical Context

  • 2.1.90 fixed rate-limit options dialog infinite loop
  • 2.1.94 fixed 429 long Retry-After causing appearance of hanging
  • 2.1.97 fixes small Retry-AAfter retry exhaustion problem

Historical Context

  • 2.1.90 fixed rate-limit options dialog infinite loop
  • 2.1.94 fixed 429 long Retry-After causing appearance of hanging
  • 2.1.97 fixes small Retry-After retry too fast

Competitor Comparison

  • All three tools encounter rate limiting
  • Claude Code has many fix records in this area, indicating they’re fine-tuning strategies at more granular level for real production traffic

Future Trend Prediction

  • May later add smarter per-model, per-endpoint, per-plan retry strategies
  • May also deeper integrate with UI, clearly telling users “I’m backing off and retrying, not stuck”

15. Context Compaction Causing Rate-limit Upgrade Options to Disappear

Section titled “15. Context Compaction Causing Rate-limit Upgrade Options to Disappear”

Problem Background

  • After being rate limited, system may suggest upgrade options or alternatives
  • But after context compaction, these prompts disappeared

Root Cause

  • UI state and session state not uniformly persisted

Impact

  • Users handling limit issues, then prompts disappear themselves, breaking experience

This group is one of the most important areas in this version, because they directly relate to whether Claude Code can become a “long-term continuous work agent”.

16. Multiple /resume Picker Issues Fixed

VI. Hook, Subagent & Compaction Related

20. Stop/SubagentStop Hooks Fail in Long Sessions, Error Messages Distorted

Section titled “20. Stop/SubagentStop Hooks Fail in Long Sessions, Error Messages Distorted”

Problem Background

  • Simultaneously API errors incorrectly displayed as “JSON validation failed”

21. Worktree Isolation or cwd: Override Subagent Leaking Working Directory Back to Parent Bash

Section titled “21. Worktree Isolation or cwd: Override Subagent Leaking Working Directory Back to Parent Bash”

Problem Background

22. Prompt-too-long Retry Repeatedly Writing Multi-MB Subagent Transcript

Section titled “22. Prompt-too-long Retry Repeatedly Writing Multi-MB Subagent Transcript”

Problem Background

  • Context too long triggers compaction/retry
  • Subagent transcript repeatedly written as multiple large files

Impact

  • Wastes disk
  • Amplifies transcript volume
  • Increases resume and IO overhead

Significance

  • Indicates compaction and subagent transcript pipeline had duplicate side effects in long sessions

23. Git-based Marketplace Plugin Updates Misreport “Already at Latest Version”

Section titled “23. Git-based Marketplace Plugin Updates Misreport “Already at Latest Version””

  • Remote already has new commits
  • Local update misreports already latest

Impact

  • Actually stuck in old code, problem hard to troubleshoot

  • Plugins under development

  • If plugin frontmatter name not properly handled, picker crashes

Example

Notes

  • For platform, this input should be safely normalized, not crashing UI

33. Bedrock SigV4 Authentication Failure When Environment Variables Set to Empty String

Section titled “33. Bedrock SigV4 Authentication Failure When Environment Variables Set to Empty String”

Problem Background

  • AWS_BEARER_TOKEN_BEDROCK or ANTHROPIC_BEDROCK_BASE_URL if empty string, previously caused SigV4 authentication failure

Use Cases

  • GitHub Actions
  • CI/CD pipelines
  • Calling Claude through Bedrock

Why Important

  • Directly impacts automated deployment and enterprise pipelines

Historical Context

  • 2.1.94 added Mantle support and continued expanding Bedrock paths
  • 2.1.96 just fixed Bedrock 403 Authorization header regression
  • 2.1.97 fixes another Bedrock authentication edge problem

34. Accept Edits Auto-approves Safe Env Prefix or Wrapper Commands

Section titled “34. Accept Edits Auto-approves Safe Env Prefix or Wrapper Commands”

Change Content

  • Commands like LANG=C rm foo
  • timeout 5 mkdir out Now auto-approved in Accept Edits mode

Problem Background

  • These prefixes themselves don’t add risk, just changing locale, timeout control, or wrapper execution

Significance

  • Reduces friction
  • Makes permission system better understand real shell world

Section titled “36. sandbox.network.allowMachLookup Effective on macOS”

  • Very significant for sandbox boundaries

Scenario

Significance

38. CJK Period Punctuation Also Triggers Slash Command / @ Mention Completion

  • Previously required space, clearly English-centric assumption

Section titled “40. Footer Indicators Fixed on Mode-indicator Line”

Section titled “41. Context-low Warning Becomes Transient Footer Notification”

42. Transcript Volume Optimization: Skip Empty Hook Entries, Limit Pre-edit File Copies

Section titled “42. Transcript Volume Optimization: Skip Empty Hook Entries, Limit Pre-edit File Copies”

  • Hooks and pre-edit copies easily become inflation sources

43. Transcript Accuracy Improvement: Record Final Token Usage Per Chunk

45. /claude-api Skill Updated, Covering Managed Agents

Section titled “45. /claude-api Skill Updated, Covering Managed Agents”

  • Claude API no longer just single model calls, but increasingly agent management and enterprise orchestration capabilities

  • Managed Agents clear future direction signal

XII. Cross-version Context Summary

Section titled “XII. Cross-version Context Summary”

Looking at 2.1.89 to 2.1.97 together, this evolution mainline very clear:

Mainline 1: NO_FLICKER from Experimental to Mainstream

Section titled “Mainline 1: NO_FLICKER from Experimental to Mainstream”
  • 2.1.89 introduced
  • Afterwards continuously fixed scrolling, copying, rendering, shortcuts, memory leaks
  • 2.1.97 starting to add “workflow-level features” like Focus View

Mainline 2: Permission System from Static Rules to Enterprise Governance

Section titled “Mainline 2: Permission System from Static Rules to Enterprise Governance”
  • Bash/PowerShell continuous hardening
  • Managed settings refresh and revocation fixes
  • additionalDirectories multi-source merging fixes
  • worktree/cwd isolation fixes

Mainline 3: /resume and Transcript Becoming Real Production Capability

Section titled “Mainline 3: /resume and Transcript Becoming Real Production Capability”
  • Multiple versions fixing transcript chain breaks, cache misses, history loss, recovery UI problems
  • Indicates Claude Code values “long-cycle continuous collaboration” highly

Mainline 4: MCP & Enterprise Cloud Integration Entering Deep Waters

Section titled “Mainline 4: MCP & Enterprise Cloud Integration Entering Deep Waters”
  • SSE performance
  • Memory leaks
  • OAuth refresh
  • Bedrock / ADFS / managed settings
  • These aren’t problems toy users encounter first, but high-frequency enterprise use exposes

XIII. Higher-level Comparison with Codex, Gemini CLI

Section titled “XIII. Higher-level Comparison with Codex, Gemini CLI”

Claude Code Characteristics

Section titled “Claude Code Characteristics”
  • Values session continuity more
  • Values permission governance and enterprise compliance more
  • Values multi-agent, worktree, resume, hooks, MCP combination capabilities more
  • Terminal UI more complex, therefore also more prone to expose rendering detail problems

Codex CLI Characteristics

Section titled “Codex CLI Characteristics”
  • Iterates extremely fast
  • Usually lighter, more direct
  • In many scenarios more “command execution and code agent” simple experience
  • Emphasis on complex UI and long session history management not as strong as Claude Code

Gemini CLI Characteristics

Section titled “Gemini CLI Characteristics”
  • Extension ecosystem very active
  • MCP/Extensions, Cloud, IDE plugin, JSON output, prompt completion etc. capabilities advancing fast
  • More like open platform CLI
  • But in long-term transcript recovery, multi-layer permission governance, subagent/worktree engineering deep waters, Claude Code product trajectory clearer

XIV. Future Evolution Trend Predictions

Section titled “XIV. Future Evolution Trend Predictions”

1. NO_FLICKER Likely Gradually Default

Section titled “1. NO_FLICKER Likely Gradually Default”

Because it’s no longer just solving flickering, but carrying new interaction capabilities.

2. Resume / Transcript System Will Continue Refactoring

Section titled “2. Resume / Transcript System Will Continue Refactoring”

Too many fixes in this area, indicating current format and process still have structural debt.

3. Multi-agent + Worktree Will Become Claude Code’s Core Differentiation

Section titled “3. Multi-agent + Worktree Will Become Claude Code’s Core Differentiation”

This path resembles “AI programming operating system”.

4. Permission System May Continue Declarative or Even Policy Language

Section titled “4. Permission System May Continue Declarative or Even Policy Language”

Especially combined with Cedar highlighting, managed settings, enterprise governance needs, resembles moving toward policy-driven agent execution.

5. Enterprise Observability & Auditability Will Continue Strengthening

Section titled “5. Enterprise Observability & Auditability Will Continue Strengthening”

OTEL tracing, managed settings, Bedrock, ADFS, these are what enterprise customers truly care about.

Final Conclusion

Section titled “Final Conclusion”

Claude Code 2.1.97 isn’t a “flashy feature version”, but a version strengthening core workflows to be more trustworthy, stable, enterprise-grade.

One sentence summary:

It’s continuing to push Claude Code from “very useful AI coding tool” toward “sustainable, governable, recoverable, observable AI development workbench”.

For ordinary individual users, this version’s most direct perception will be:

  • NO_FLICKER smoother
  • Permission prompts more reasonable
  • /resume more reliable
  • Chinese/Japanese input more natural

For heavy users and enterprise users, this version’s truly important aspects:

  • Permission system more consistent
  • MCP more stable
  • Transcript more trustworthy
  • Worktree/subagent isolation safer
  • Observability and cloud integration more mature
